A_target.statement: There are exactly five combinatorial types of [[Definition:Platonic Solid|regular convex polyhedra]], with face and vertex types $\set {p, q}$ equal to $\set {3, 3}$, $\set {3, 4}$, $\set {4, 3}$, $\set {3, 5}$ and $\set {5, 3}$.

B_source.statement:
Let $P$ be a [[Definition:Convex Polyhedron|convex polyhedron]] with $V$ vertices, $E$ edges and $F$ faces.
Then:
:$V - E + F = 2$

substitutions.V, E, F: expressions in E, p and q

object_map.reformulation: Count incidences to express V and F through E, and substitute into Euler's formula.

validity_conditions: Every face has p sides and every vertex has degree q, with p, q >= 3.
Euler's formula only constrains the combinatorics; existence of the five solids is shown by construction.
proof_plan:
Counting edge-face and edge-vertex incidences:
:$p F = 2 E = q V$

Substituting into $V - E + F = 2$:
:$\dfrac {2 E} q - E + \dfrac {2 E} p = 2$, that is, $\dfrac 1 p + \dfrac 1 q = \dfrac 1 2 + \dfrac 1 E > \dfrac 1 2$

This is equivalent to $\paren {p - 2} \paren {q - 2} < 4$.
With $p, q \ge 3$ the only solutions are $\tuple {3, 3}$, $\tuple {3, 4}$, $\tuple {4, 3}$, $\tuple {3, 5}$, $\tuple {5, 3}$.

These give $E = 6, 12, 12, 30, 30$, realized by the tetrahedron, octahedron, cube, icosahedron and dodecahedron.
{{qed}}
